meta.title: Install TNP -- The Network Protocol
meta.description: Set up TNP to resolve TNP domains on any device. Install the TNP client, or forward .ox to the TNP resolver.
meta.ogDescription: Set up TNP to resolve TNP domains on any device.

title: Set Up TNP
subtitle: Resolve TNP domains on any device. Pick a method below.

facts: The TNP resolver at {{dnsIp}} answers plain DNS on port 53 (UDP and TCP).
It is not encrypted and has no DNS-over-TLS. The TNP operator, and anyone on the network path, can see the .ox names you look up.
The steps below forward only .ox to it. Everything else keeps going to the resolver you use today, so your other lookups never reach TNP.
dns.clientHint: On a computer, <clientLink>install the TNP client</clientLink> instead if you can: it resolves .ox on your machine over HTTPS and routes only .ox to itself.

router.title: Router or network resolver
router.intro: Forward .ox where your network already resolves names. Every device that uses it, phones included, can then resolve .ox, and all other lookups keep going to the router's usual upstream.

basic.title: Routers that only let you set primary/secondary DNS
basic.desc: Most ISP and consumer routers can only replace the DNS servers; they cannot forward one domain. Putting TNP there sends every lookup from every device on your network to TNP, unencrypted. We recommend against it. Never pair TNP with a public resolver as the secondary either: devices use either server at random, so .ox would resolve only some of the time. Run Pi-hole or AdGuard Home on your network instead, or set up each computer.

windows.title: Windows
windows.desc: In PowerShell as Administrator, add a Name Resolution Policy Table (NRPT) rule. Only .ox goes to TNP; your network adapters' DNS servers are not changed.

macos.title: macOS
macos.desc: Create a resolver file for .ox. Only .ox goes to TNP; everything else uses your current DNS. If /etc/resolver/ox already exists (the TNP client writes it), the command leaves it unchanged, and undo only removes a file these steps created.
macos.test: dig and nslookup ignore /etc/resolver. Test in a browser or with dscacheutil -q host -a name yourname.ox; scutil --dns lists the new resolver.

other.title: Older systemd-resolved, or none
other.desc: Before systemd 258 there is no delegate file, and adding TNP to an interface or to resolved.conf also sends your public lookups to TNP. A plain /etc/resolv.conf cannot route by domain at all, so never put TNP's address in it. <clientLink>Install the TNP client</clientLink>: on older systemd-resolved it sets up a dedicated link that receives only .ox.

mobile.title: Android and iOS
points: Phones cannot send a single domain to a different resolver without an app, so there are no per-phone steps.

<routerLink>Forward .ox on your router</routerLink> instead. Every phone on that network then resolves .ox, and all other lookups keep going to your router's usual resolver. On mobile data or other networks, .ox will not resolve.
Do not enter a TNP name in Android's Private DNS. Private DNS is DNS-over-TLS, which the TNP resolver does not offer, so every lookup on the phone would fail.
Setting TNP as a Wi-Fi network's manual DNS would send every lookup on that network to TNP, unencrypted. We recommend against it.

client.intro: The client only intercepts TNP domains -- your regular DNS stays unchanged. This is the recommended setup for desktop devices.

macos.title: macOS
macos.description: The client runs a local DNS proxy that intercepts only TNP domains. All other DNS queries go through your normal resolver untouched.
requirements: Admin password (the installer sets up a resolver config)

linux.title: Linux
linux.description: The client uses systemd-resolved to send only .ox to its local resolver: a DNS delegate on systemd 258 or later, a dedicated link on older versions. Your other DNS settings are not touched. Without systemd-resolved it changes nothing and tells you how to forward .ox in your own resolver.
requirements: A Linux distribution with systemd-resolved (for automatic DNS setup)

serve.intro: Make any local service accessible over the TNP overlay network. No port forwarding, no public IP, no firewall configuration needed.
serve.heading: Host a Service
serve.step2Desc: This opens a browser window for SSO. Your token is stored locally and reused for subsequent commands.
serve.step3Desc: Replace <code1>example.ox</code1> with your registered domain and <code2>localhost:80</code2> with the local address of your service.
howItWorksList: The client connects to a relay server and registers your domain as a service node.
Incoming requests to your domain are routed through the relay over an encrypted tunnel.
Your local service receives traffic as if it were served locally -- no exposure to the public internet.
The connection is kept alive with periodic heartbeats. If the client disconnects, the domain goes offline.

relay.intro: Relays are the backbone of the TNP overlay network. They route encrypted traffic between clients and service nodes.
whatRelaysDoList: Accept connections from service nodes and hold them open as tunnels.
Route incoming client requests to the correct service node over those tunnels.
Encrypt all traffic end-to-end -- the relay never sees plaintext data.
Report liveness and capacity to the TNP registry for load balancing.
relay.communityRelayDesc: Community relays help grow the network and improve performance for everyone. You need a server with a public IP and a stable connection.
relay.step3Desc: The relay automatically registers itself with the TNP registry on startup. It will appear on the <link>network status page</link> once active.
relay.githubNote: See the <link>GitHub repository</link> for full documentation and configuration options.
